Influenza A(H5N1) - United States of America 24 November 2026 See all DONs related to this event Situation at a glance Between 16 October and 4 November 2026, the United States of America, through its International Health Regulations (IHR) National Focal Point, notified WHO of three laboratory-confirmed human infections with influenza A(H5) virus in Washington State. These included one fatal case, the first reported death following exposure to infected dairy cattle or a related contaminated environment. All three cases were adults who worked on dairy cattle farms in Yakima County, Washington State, where the highly pathogenic (in animals) avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus had recently been detected in dairy cattle. Investigations and monitoring of exposed people and close contacts are ongoing. Based on information available to date, there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission. In accordance with the IHR (2005), any human infection caused by a new influenza A virus subtype is considered a potentially significant public health event and is subject to mandatory notification to WHO. Based on the information currently available on this and previous cases, WHO assesses the risk to the general population posed by A(H5N1) viruses as low. For individuals with occupational exposure to these viruses, the risk of infection is considered low to moderate. The situation may change as more information becomes available. WHO continues to closely monitor these viruses and the global epidemiological situation. Description of the situation On 16 October 2026, WHO was notified by the United States of America's International Health Regulations' National Focal Point of a laboratory-confirmed human infection with influenza A(H5) virus in Washington State. On 4 November 2026, two additional laboratory-confirmed human infections in the same state, including one fatal case, were notified to WHO. All three cases were adults aged 18 years or older who worked in Yakima County, Washington State, a major agricultural and dairy-producing area, where HPAI A(H5N1) virus had recently been detected in dairy cattle. It is not known if the cases worked on the same farm. The first case developed symptoms on 5 October 2026, including eye irritation, runny nose, muscle aches and headache, and sought medical care on 12 October. The case was not hospitalized and was offered treatment with oseltamivir. Eye (conjunctival) and nose and throat (nasopharyngeal) specimens were collected on 12 October and tested at the Washington State Public Health Laboratory using the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza A(H5) assay on 14 October. The conjunctival specimen tested positive for influenza A(H5) virus. Additional testing conducted by CDC determined this was an influenza A(H5N1) virus. The second case, who had underlying medical conditions, developed respiratory symptoms during epidemiological week 42, ending on 24 October 2026. The case presented to an emergency department the following week, was hospitalized with severe illness and died on 1 November. A respiratory specimen collected at the healthcare facility tested positive for influenza A virus and yielded a presumptive positive result for influenza A(H5) at the University of Washington. The Washington State Public Health Laboratory subsequently confirmed influenza A(H5) virus infection using the CDC influenza A(H5) assay. Further testing at the University of Washington identified the virus as influenza A(H5N1). The third case developed conjunctivitis and sought medical care but did not require hospitalization.
